name: Byzantine Fault Tolerance
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: When Some of the Machines Are Lying to You
lesson.summary: Byzantine fault tolerance is a distributed system's ability to keep reaching correct agreement even when some participants send conflicting or malicious messages rather than simply going silent.
lesson.body:
Distributed systems research has long dealt with machines that fail, but failure comes in different flavors, and the difference matters enormously. A crash fault is polite: a machine just stops responding, and everyone else can eventually notice and work around it. A Byzantine fault is not polite at all. A faulty participant might send different, contradictory messages to different peers, claim to have received something it never got, or actively try to steer the group toward the wrong answer. Byzantine fault tolerance is the property of a system that keeps reaching the correct, consistent outcome even when some participants behave exactly this badly.

This distinction matters directly for the consensus mechanisms described earlier. A blockchain has no way to vet who is running a node before letting them participate, and it has to assume that some fraction of participants might be actively adversarial rather than just unreliable, whether out of greed, sabotage, or a simple bug that happens to produce dangerous behavior. A consensus mechanism that only tolerates honest mistakes and silent crashes is not enough for that environment. It needs to survive participants who are actively trying to break it.

A classic result from this field gives a concrete sense of the limits involved: in the standard model used for this kind of fault tolerance, a system can only guarantee correct agreement if strictly fewer than one third of participants are Byzantine, meaning you generally need more than two thirds of the total group to be honest and following the rules for the system to work reliably. Push past that fraction of bad actors and no protocol in this model can guarantee that honest participants will still agree with each other, no matter how cleverly it is designed.

A useful mental picture is a company with twelve regional offices that must all agree on the same final sales number before headquarters can close the books, using only messages passed between offices with no central switchboard. If three of those offices are compromised and start sending different numbers to different peers, honest offices following a Byzantine fault tolerant procedure can still cross check enough messages to converge on the true number. Push the number of compromised offices to five out of twelve, comfortably above the one third line, and that guarantee breaks down.

Byzantine fault tolerance is not itself one specific algorithm, it is a property a system either has or does not have, and a design goal that different consensus mechanisms pursue in different ways. Proof of work pursues it indirectly, by making dishonest behavior expensive rather than mathematically bounded by a fraction of participants. The next two chapters look at the classic thought experiment that gave this problem its name, and the specific practical protocol that made Byzantine fault tolerant agreement fast enough for real systems to use.
